title: Lakehouse architecture: storage is not the whole system
summary: Separate durable data, table semantics, compute and serving so an architecture diagram explains responsibilities rather than logos.
objectives: Identify storage, table, compute and serving responsibilities.
Explain bronze, silver and gold as refinement stages.
Connect a consumer requirement to a suitable serving boundary.
prerequisites: Comfort reading a small table; no running cloud service is required.

blocks.title: The problem this solves
blocks.text: A lakehouse diagram often begins with object storage and ends with a dashboard, but the important design decisions are in between. Raw files need interpretation, updates need reliable table semantics, transformations need compute and users need an appropriate serving path. A folder called gold is not automatically trustworthy. The architecture should explain how data becomes validated, how changes are applied and what guarantees consumers can rely on.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.text: Storage preserves bytes; a table format adds metadata and table-level behavior such as snapshots or transactions according to its implementation. Compute reads and transforms the data. Catalog and governance services help identify and control access to assets. Serving makes prepared data usable through SQL, semantic models, applications or other interfaces. Medallion stages are a useful refinement pattern: raw capture, validated integration and business-ready outputs, not three mandatory physical copies of every dataset.
blocks.mentalModel: A lakehouse is a workshop around a durable stockroom. The stockroom holds material, workbenches transform it, and the delivery counter exposes products under a clear contract.

blocks.title: Follow the flow

diagram.label: Lakehouse architecture: storage is not the whole system - a simplified teaching flow

blocks.caption: Read each box as a responsibility or state, not as a mandatory product. The arrows show the order of reasoning; a real implementation can have additional checks and branches.

steps.title: Preserve recoverable input
steps.text: Keep enough source identity and ingestion metadata to explain where a row came from and to replay a bounded interval when permitted.

steps.title: Define refinement contracts
steps.text: At each stage, specify keys, accepted schema, quality rules and treatment of rejected records. A naming convention does not enforce these rules.

steps.title: Design for consumption
steps.text: Choose the output grain and serving interface from actual use cases. A dashboard summary, a data-science feature table and an operational API may need different outputs.

blocks.title: A small concrete example
blocks.code:
bronze_orders: source rows + ingestion identity
silver_orders: validated keys + normalized amounts
gold_daily_sales: one row per business date and region

Each published table records:
  grain | owner | quality gate | freshness | access policy
blocks.caption: This sketch is platform-neutral. Delta, Iceberg and other table technologies have different feature and interoperability details that must be verified for the selected engines.

blocks.title: Keep these distinctions clear
rows: Storage
Where are durable bytes kept?
Files alone provide every table-level guarantee
Table semantics
How are snapshots and changes represented?
Every engine supports every format feature equally
Compute
Where do transformations and queries execute?
Shared storage makes all workloads resource-independent
Serving
How do consumers access meaningful outputs?
A raw table is already a governed business model

blocks.title: Reason through the example
steps: A retailer receives order changes from several systems. Bronze retains source records with origin and ingestion identifiers.
Silver standardizes amounts and keys, selects valid current versions and keeps rejected records visible to operators.
Gold creates daily regional sales at an explicitly declared grain. Its publication depends on reconciliation and completeness checks.
A BI semantic model defines reusable measures over gold. An investigation tool may use controlled silver access instead of trying to recover transaction details from an aggregated gold table.
blocks.result: Different consumers get appropriate products from the same refinement chain without confusing raw capture with certified analytical meaning.

items.signal: Several workloads need access to durable shared data
items.choice: Separate storage and table contracts from the compute engines consuming them.

items.signal: Data moves from raw capture to business reporting
items.choice: Use explicit refinement stages and publication gates, even if physical implementation differs by platform.

blocks.title: A mistake worth catching
blocks.text: Treating bronze, silver and gold as mandatory folders can create copies without improving quality. Conversely, overwriting raw input too early can make failures difficult to reproduce.
blocks.correction: Give every stage a reason: recoverability, validation, integration or serving. Keep only the copies and retention that support those responsibilities and governance requirements.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.question: A table is stored in a folder named gold but has duplicate business keys and no freshness check. Is it business-ready?
blocks.answer: Not merely because of its folder name.
blocks.explanation: Readiness is established by a documented grain, tests, ownership and a consumer contract. A medallion label describes intended responsibility, not proof that the responsibility was fulfilled.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Separate storage, table semantics, compute and serving.
Refinement stages need real contracts, not only names.
Choose output grain and access paths from consumer needs.

title: Compare platforms by constraints, not by a winner
summary: Build a defensible Fabric, Databricks, Snowflake and BigQuery comparison around workload, team, governance and cost assumptions.
objectives: Separate common responsibilities from product-specific integration.
Choose comparison dimensions that matter to a real workload.
Explain why a benchmark must state its assumptions.
prerequisites: Comfort reading a small table; no running cloud service is required.

blocks.title: The problem this solves
blocks.text: “Which platform is best?” is usually the wrong first question. A small Power BI team, a Spark-heavy engineering group and a SQL analytics organization may value different operational paths. All need dependable ingestion, transformation, governance and consumption, but they do not need the same combination of interfaces or controls. A useful comparison starts with constraints and an existing estate, then tests a small representative workload instead of relying on a feature checklist.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.text: Fabric emphasizes an integrated Microsoft analytics experience including OneLake and Power BI. Databricks provides a lakehouse-oriented platform with strong data-engineering and machine-learning workflows. Snowflake separates storage, compute and cloud-service responsibilities in its architecture. BigQuery is a managed Google Cloud analytical service with its own compute, storage and operating model. These descriptions are orientation points, not exclusive capability boundaries or permanent pricing claims.
blocks.mentalModel: Compare routes to the same destination. The shortest route depends on where the team starts, what it carries and which checkpoints it must pass.

blocks.title: Follow the flow

diagram.label: Compare platforms by constraints, not by a winner - a simplified teaching flow

blocks.caption: Read each box as a responsibility or state, not as a mandatory product. The arrows show the order of reasoning; a real implementation can have additional checks and branches.

steps.title: Define a workload envelope
steps.text: Record data volume and shape, refresh frequency, query concurrency, latency expectations and the expected engineering skill set.

steps.title: Compare full operating paths
steps.text: Include identity, catalog, deployment, observability, recovery and serving integration. A fast isolated query is only one part of the cost and reliability story.

steps.title: Test the uncertain assumptions
steps.text: Run a small representative benchmark and document cache state, dataset, configuration and pricing basis. Avoid declaring a universal winner from a favorable default demo.

blocks.title: A small concrete example
blocks.code:
Requirement: daily sales + interactive BI
Must have: governed access, replayable loads, known freshness
Existing skills: SQL, Python, Power BI
Compare: end-to-end build effort, query experience, operations
Measure: correctness, latency, refresh, resource consumption
Record: assumptions, unsupported needs, exit / migration costs
blocks.caption: No current price, quota or service-level guarantee is asserted here. Verify the exact region, edition, capacity and contract before a purchasing or migration decision.

blocks.title: Keep these distinctions clear
columns: Question for your proof of concept
rows: Fabric
Integrated Microsoft analytics and BI path
Does the supported serving mode fit the data and capacity?
Databricks
Lakehouse engineering, Spark and ML workflows
Which compute and governance choices fit the team?
Snowflake
Managed SQL analytics with separated responsibilities
How do workload isolation and consumption behave?
BigQuery
Managed analytical SQL in Google Cloud
How do query shape and the chosen pricing model affect operations?

blocks.title: Reason through the example
steps: Team A already owns governed Power BI reports and needs a daily financial summary. Integration and semantic-model ownership are major comparison dimensions.
Team B processes complex event data with Spark and maintains ML pipelines. Engineering and model-lifecycle workflows carry more weight for that workload.
Both teams run the same correctness checks on a sample dataset, but their evaluation scores need not use identical weights.
A recommendation records which assumptions would reverse the decision, such as a new cloud restriction, a different concurrency profile or a material change in team skills.
blocks.result: The comparison becomes explainable because it ties platform choices to concrete constraints and acknowledges the cost of alternatives.

items.signal: A team is choosing or consolidating a platform
items.choice: Use a weighted decision record grounded in actual workloads and operational ownership.

items.signal: A current platform seems expensive or slow
items.choice: Investigate workload design and configuration before assuming migration is the only remedy.

blocks.title: A mistake worth catching
blocks.text: Comparing one warm cached query on one platform with a cold full scan on another does not support a fair performance conclusion. Feature names also hide differences in limits and operational responsibility.
blocks.correction: Publish the benchmark conditions and compare equivalent business outcomes. Use current primary documentation for capabilities and a measured trial for the uncertain workload behavior.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.question: Should the platform with the shortest isolated query time automatically win the architecture decision?
blocks.answer: No. Query latency is one dimension among correctness, integration, governance, reliability and total operating effort.
blocks.explanation: A faster query may come with a poor deployment path or an unsuitable cost profile for the real concurrency pattern. The decision must match the whole workload and organization.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Start with constraints and existing capabilities.
Compare end-to-end operating paths, not only product features.
State benchmark conditions and the assumptions behind the decision.

title: Distributed compute: partitions, skew and small files
summary: Diagnose uneven work before adding more machines, and distinguish a hot partition from an excess of tiny tasks.
objectives: Explain why one long task can dominate a distributed stage.
Distinguish data skew from a small-file problem.
Match a measured bottleneck to a targeted intervention.
prerequisites: Comfort reading a small table; no running cloud service is required.

blocks.title: The problem this solves
blocks.text: A distributed job finishes only when its required work finishes. If most tasks complete quickly but one task handles a dominant key, the stage can remain slow even with many idle cores. Another job may spend its time opening thousands of tiny files and scheduling short tasks. Both are performance problems, but they need different diagnoses. “Add workers” is not an explanation of either problem and may waste resources without changing the bottleneck.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.text: Partitions determine units of distributed work, but equal partition counts do not guarantee equal work. Skew occurs when some keys or partitions receive disproportionately much data or expensive computation. Small files introduce metadata, scheduling and file-open overhead relative to useful processing. Adaptive execution and engine optimizations can help in supported situations, but their effect must be checked in the actual plan and metrics.
blocks.mentalModel: A group assignment finishes at the pace of its slowest required member. Giving everyone another chair does not divide one person's oversized task.

blocks.title: Follow the flow

diagram.label: Distributed compute: partitions, skew and small files - a simplified teaching flow

blocks.caption: Read each box as a responsibility or state, not as a mandatory product. The arrows show the order of reasoning; a real implementation can have additional checks and branches.

steps.title: Inspect distributions
steps.text: Look at task duration, input bytes, shuffle bytes and spill, not just total duration. A large maximum relative to typical tasks suggests uneven work.

steps.title: Check key and file shape
steps.text: Profile dominant grouping or join keys and file-size distributions. Confirm whether the time is spent processing one hot key or coordinating too many tiny inputs.

steps.title: Apply a specific remedy
steps.text: Consider pre-aggregation, a different join strategy, appropriate partitioning or compaction according to the measured cause. Retest correctness as well as speed.

blocks.title: A small concrete example
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Find candidate hot keys before choosing a skew strategy.
(events.groupBy('customer_id')
       .count()
       .orderBy(F.desc('count'))
       .show(10))

# Also inspect the physical plan and stage metrics.
# Do not add repartition() merely because it is available.
blocks.caption: The profiling query itself performs distributed work. Run it on an appropriate sample or environment and include its cost in the investigation. This app does not start a Spark cluster.

blocks.title: Keep these distinctions clear
rows: One task is much slower than the rest
Skew or unusually expensive records
Per-key counts, partition sizes and task metrics
Many tiny tasks with little data
Small-file or scheduling overhead
File count, file size and scan planning time
Heavy spill across tasks
Memory pressure or oversized partitions
Row width, partition size and aggregation state
Large shuffle traffic
Expensive redistribution
Join plan, filtering and pre-aggregation opportunities

blocks.title: Reason through the example
steps: A stage has 100 tasks. Ninety-nine finish in about 8 seconds, while one takes 4 minutes and reads much more data.
The hot task contains a default customer key used for a large share of unmatched events. Doubling worker count does not automatically split that key's aggregation.

The team investigates whether the default-key records should be separated, whether a supported skew strategy applies, or whether partial aggregation can reduce the exchange. Each option must preserve the intended total.
A different pipeline has no long tail but opens 80,000 tiny files. Its investigation focuses on file layout and compaction rather than on customer-key salting.
blocks.result: The intervention follows the measured shape of the work instead of treating every slow distributed job as a shortage of machines.

items.signal: Task duration has a very large tail
items.choice: Investigate skew and expensive partitions before scaling the cluster.
Investigate file sizing and write patterns; do not merge everything into a single giant file.

blocks.title: A mistake worth catching
blocks.text: Blindly coalescing to one partition can remove parallelism and create a new bottleneck. Salting a key without a correct recombination step can also change the meaning of an aggregate.
blocks.correction: State how the proposed change redistributes work and how the final result remains equivalent. Compare against the same dataset and representative query after the change.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.question: Most tasks are idle while one hot-key task runs. Why may adding workers fail to improve the stage?
blocks.answer: The remaining work is concentrated in one task rather than evenly available to the new workers.
blocks.explanation: Extra capacity helps only when work can use it. The key distribution or physical plan may need to change before additional workers can process the bottleneck in parallel.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Distributed performance depends on work distribution, not just worker count.
Skew and small files are distinct problems.
Measure task and data shape, then validate a targeted change.

title: Access boundaries: identity, permissions and state
summary: Trace who can do what at each layer, and treat deployment state and logs as sensitive parts of the data system.
objectives: Identify storage, compute and serving access boundaries.
Explain why hidden UI values can still exist in state or logs.
prerequisites: Comfort reading a small table; no running cloud service is required.

blocks.title: The problem this solves
blocks.text: A secure architecture cannot be inferred from the presence of a login screen. The same data can be reachable through storage, a query endpoint, a semantic model, an export or a deployment artifact. Each path needs an identity and an authorization decision. A report that hides a column does not necessarily prevent direct access to the underlying table. Likewise, a tool that masks a secret in its console may still retain that secret in state.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.text: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides which actions that identity may perform on which resources. Least privilege limits those permissions to the required scope. Governance adds ownership, classification, lineage and lifecycle expectations. Infrastructure state can include sensitive resource attributes, so its storage, encryption, access and recovery controls matter alongside the deployed system itself. Marking a value sensitive is not the same as ensuring it never exists in persisted state.
blocks.mentalModel: Every door needs its own key policy. Hiding a room on the building map does not lock the door, and the maintenance office may hold keys that are just as sensitive as the rooms.

blocks.title: Follow the flow

diagram.label: Access boundaries: identity, permissions and state - a simplified teaching flow

blocks.caption: Read each box as a responsibility or state, not as a mandatory product. The arrows show the order of reasoning; a real implementation can have additional checks and branches.

steps.title: Enumerate access paths
steps.text: List human users, service identities, administrators and automated jobs. Include exports, state files, backups and diagnostic logs, not just the main application.

steps.title: Define minimum rights
steps.text: Separate read, write and administrative privileges. Scope a pipeline identity to the data and operations it needs instead of granting broad ownership by default.

steps.title: Test as the intended identity
steps.text: A successful administrator test proves little about reader restrictions. Verify allowed and denied operations with representative identities and record auditable outcomes without exposing secrets.

blocks.title: A small concrete example
blocks.code:
Identity: daily-orders-loader
Allowed: read landing/orders, write trusted/orders
Denied: read payroll, change access policies
Secrets: retrieved through an approved secret mechanism
State: restricted backend, encryption and recovery policy
Evidence: successful allowed action + rejected denied action
blocks.caption: This is a design checklist, not an access policy for a specific cloud. Exact identity and permission semantics depend on the platform and resource type.

blocks.title: Keep these distinctions clear
rows: Authentication
Who is making the request?
A login automatically grants the correct scope
Authorization
Which resource actions are permitted?
A hidden menu item prevents API access
Serving layer
What can this reader query or export?
A report-only test covers direct table access
State and logs
Where can sensitive values persist?
Masked output means no secret is stored anywhere

blocks.title: Reason through the example
steps: A BI reader is allowed to view approved sales summaries but not raw payroll data. The report interface exposes only sales pages.
The team also checks the reader's direct storage and SQL permissions, because those paths can bypass the report interface.
A deployment identity provisions resources. Its state backend is restricted and protected, since state may contain sensitive attributes even when command output is masked.
An incident drill verifies that the team can revoke an identity, inspect audit evidence and restore required encrypted state using the approved key-recovery process.
blocks.result: The security argument covers real access paths and operational artifacts instead of relying on the appearance of the user interface.

items.signal: A new ingestion or reporting path is introduced
items.choice: Review identity and permissions at every boundary, including exports and diagnostics.
Protect plan and state artifacts as part of the system, and verify the encryption and recovery configuration actually used.

blocks.title: A mistake worth catching
blocks.text: Copying raw state or logs into a public issue or source repository can expose secrets and internal identifiers. Encryption also creates a recovery dependency: losing the required key can make protected state unusable.
blocks.correction: Keep sensitive artifacts out of public deliverables, use restricted storage, and test a documented recovery path. Share redacted evidence rather than raw production state.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.question: A secret is masked in a deployment tool's output. Can you assume it is absent from the tool's saved state?
blocks.answer: No. Display masking and persisted-state protection are different controls.
blocks.explanation: Review what the tool stores and how the backend protects it. Use appropriate encryption, access restriction and retention; do not publish state because its console output looked harmless.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Review every data path, not only the main UI.
Protect state, logs and backups with explicit access and recovery controls.

title: Operate with evidence: cost, reliability and recovery
summary: Use a small diagnostic loop to connect symptoms to measurements, make a bounded change and verify the result.
objectives: Separate user-visible symptoms from a proposed cause.
Use query and service evidence before changing capacity.
Define a reversible intervention and a success measure.
prerequisites: Comfort reading a small table; no running cloud service is required.

blocks.title: The problem this solves
blocks.text: Operational work often begins with a vague symptom: the report is expensive, the service is unreachable or the daily job is late. Jumping immediately to a larger machine or a restart may hide the real cause. A better loop states the expected behavior, gathers a few decisive measurements, forms a hypothesis and changes one thing at a time. Reliability and cost should be evaluated together: a cheap query that misses its deadline is not necessarily a good design.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.text: Cost depends on the platform's charging model and the work actually performed. Reliability depends on whether the service meets its intended behavior over time and can recover from failure. Performance measurements help connect both to specific mechanisms. For a query, investigate scanned data, partition pruning and execution shape. For a service, follow the request path through names, selectors, endpoints and listening ports before assuming that more replicas will help.
blocks.mentalModel: Diagnose like a mechanic: describe the symptom, inspect the relevant gauges, test one hypothesis, and verify the repair under the same conditions.

blocks.title: Follow the flow

diagram.label: Operate with evidence: cost, reliability and recovery - a simplified teaching flow

blocks.caption: Read each box as a responsibility or state, not as a mandatory product. The arrows show the order of reasoning; a real implementation can have additional checks and branches.

steps.title: Make the symptom measurable
steps.text: Replace “slow” with a defined query, input interval and observed latency. Replace “expensive” with the relevant resource or billing measure under the chosen pricing model.

steps.title: Trace the actual path
steps.text: For partitioned data, check whether the query filters the partitioning field in a supported way. For a service, verify selected endpoints and port mapping before changing replica counts.

steps.title: Test and record the change
steps.text: Use a representative before-and-after comparison. Keep a rollback path and monitor for regressions in correctness, latency, availability and consumption.

blocks.title: A small concrete example
blocks.code:
-- Select only needed columns and the required date interval.
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM daily_sales
WHERE business_date = DATE '2026-01-15'
GROUP BY region;

-- Before execution: inspect the plan / estimate where supported.
-- After execution: record result checks, latency and resource use.
-- For a service: inspect selector -> endpoints -> target port.
blocks.caption: The SQL is generic. In BigQuery, use the tools and cost controls appropriate to the selected pricing model; a LIMIT alone is not a general guarantee of a cheaper scan.

blocks.title: Keep these distinctions clear
rows: High scan consumption
Selected columns, partition filter, estimated bytes
Add LIMIT and assume the scan is now small
Service has no reachable backends
Selector labels and EndpointSlices
Add replicas with the same mismatched labels
Job misses its deadline
Critical path, retries and task distribution
Increase every task's resources equally
Frequent manual recovery
Failure classes and replay safety
Hide alerts instead of fixing repeatable causes

blocks.title: Reason through the example
steps: A daily regional query scans far more data than expected. The intended output is one business day, but the original query reads all history and filters the date only in a later client step.
The team moves the valid date restriction into the query and selects only needed columns. It checks the engine's estimate and compares actual results against the original day's output.
Separately, a service has healthy pods but no endpoints selected by its service label. The team fixes the selector mismatch instead of adding more pods.
Both changes are narrow and reversible. The record includes the hypothesis, measurements, exact configuration change and the checks that established improvement.
blocks.result: Operational changes are justified by evidence and verified against the original user-visible problem.

items.signal: A cost or latency regression appears
items.choice: Compare equivalent workloads and investigate the resource path before buying more capacity.

items.signal: A service is unreachable despite healthy processes
items.choice: Trace routing and selection boundaries; process health is only one part of reachability.

blocks.title: A mistake worth catching
blocks.text: A green process-health check does not prove the whole request path works. Similarly, a query returning ten rows may still scan a large dataset; output size and processing work are different measurements.
blocks.correction: Measure the end-to-end outcome and the relevant internal work. Avoid treating a small result or a running process as complete evidence of efficiency or reliability.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.question: A query returns ten rows after LIMIT 10. Does that prove it scanned only ten rows and therefore cost very little?
blocks.answer: No. The engine may still read much more data to produce those rows.
blocks.explanation: Inspect the query plan or estimate and actual resource metrics. Projection, partitioning, clustering and the pricing model influence cost; result-row count alone is not enough.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Trace the actual query or request path before scaling.
Make bounded, reversible changes and verify the end-to-end result.
